They were here before the pipes. Before the engines, before the stenciled letters and the junction with its faded symbol. The basin was quarried for a purpose, but it was already occupied, and the quarrymen knew it. You can see where they worked around certain formations, left channels that follow the natural contours of seepage rather than imposing order on it. The water was already moving. They did not stop it. They built their system to live alongside something that had already claimed this stone.

The small things with too many legs—these are the most visible inhabitants, the ones you will notice first. They move through the moisture like slow water, like intention without direction. Their bodies are not shells but membranes, translucent as wet paper, and within them you can see the pulse of organs that do not correspond to any anatomy you know. They have no eyes, or they have eyes everywhere, or they see through the moisture itself, tasting the chemistry of your passage. In the deep pools they gather in clusters, their bodies overlapping, and for a moment they look almost like a single creature before they separate again, flowing apart like spilled mercury.

They do not fear you. This is not courage. They have no framework for fear. You are simply another presence in a place dense with presence, another source of heat and motion and the mineral smell of your own skin. They investigate you the way you might investigate a change in light—curiously, without urgency, already forgetting as they process. One of them finds the gap between your sleeve and glove and pauses there, tasting your skin, your pulse, the boundary between inside and outside. It stays for a long moment. Then it moves on, and you cannot tell if it found you interesting or disappointing or simply a fact to be catalogued and dismissed.

The fibrous growths are older. Some of them have been here since before the quarriers, since before whatever process first brought water through this stone. They do not grow so much as *accumulate*, converting mineral and moisture into something that is neither alive nor dead in any meaningful sense. When you touch them they do not respond—they have no nervous system to respond with—but they do not resist either. They simply exist, pressing back against your finger with a softness that is almost solicitation, as though they want to be known. The crystalline deposits are their opposite, hard and glittering, growing in patterns that suggest intention without proving it. Together, the fibrous and the crystalline form a kind of skin across the stone, a membrane between the wet and the dry, and the soft-bodied things move through it freely, dissolving a path and sealing it behind them.

The engines do not belong to you or to anyone you can name. They are old—older than the stenciled letters suggest, or perhaps the letters are simply older than their makers—and they have changed in the way of things that are tended but never replaced.
